l: Make game audio respond to the world
p: AudioPhysx brings purposeful playback tools, physically inspired audio processing and world-aware Blueprint helpers into Unreal Engine. Build sound that reacts to distance, materials, motion and player actions—without turning every MetaSound into a maze of wiring.

These pages describe the UE 5.8.4 development baseline of AudioPhysx. The final Fab package, supported platforms and Shipping-build test results are still being prepared. See Compatibility for verified versus pending items.
Get your first sound playing. Install the plugin, create a MetaSound Source and build a three-part sound sequence. No C++ or acoustic setup is needed.
Find the right tool for the job. Choose between variation, sequences, distance-aware playback, acoustic effects and trigger utilities.
Connect the world to sound. Use Blueprint functions for projectile flybys, physical-material interaction and acoustic paths.

AudioPhysx is a native Unreal Engine C++ plugin. This documentation currently reflects a development build for UE 5.8.4; confirm the final supported engine versions on Compatibility before installing a commercial package.

You'll need an Unreal project with MetaSounds available, a working AudioPhysx installation, and appropriately licensed audio recordings for the playback tutorials. The more advanced acoustic and flyby workflows also need game-provided positions, traces or material data.

l: The four things you connect most often
p: Wave Asset is a reference to an imported sound recording. A Wave Asset Array holds several such references; it does not itself play multiple recordings simultaneously unless the chosen player is designed to do that.
Trigger means something happens at this moment. Play, Stop Firing and On Finished are events, not audio streams. A trigger might be issued by another MetaSound node or by a gameplay parameter/event.
Audio pins carry actual sample buffers. Out Mono is a one-channel audio stream. That mono output can be routed through additional processing and then spatialized by Unreal's broader audio system.
Control pins carry numbers, Booleans, arrays or material identifiers. For example, a player may use a Distance (cm) control to select an appropriate recording before playback begins.

l: Units are part of the contract
p: cm — centimetres. Unreal world positions are generally expressed in centimetres.
m — metres. Some AudioPhysx physical models and flyby inputs use metres instead.
m/s — metres per second; do not confuse this with Unreal's centimetres-per-second velocity values.
ms — milliseconds, one thousandth of a second.
dB — decibels, used for level or frequency-band loss. A dB number is not a linear gain multiplier.
st — semitones, a unit of musical pitch interval.
RPM — events or rounds per minute, used for the middle of Start Loop End playback.
A projectile 500 Unreal units away is typically 500 cm = 5 m. Feeding 500 directly to a pin labelled Distance (m) would be a hundredfold distance error.

l: What this plugin does not replace
p: AudioPhysx extends, rather than replaces, Unreal's core audio features. You still use MetaSound Sources, audio components, Sound Attenuation, concurrency settings and the Audio Mixer where relevant. Acoustic modelling nodes also need meaningful world data; they do not automatically know your level geometry from the audio samples alone.

We're going to create a sound that has three distinct stages: a click, a mechanical movement, and a final clunk. One Play trigger starts the action; AudioPhysx waits for each recording to finish before moving to the next. You won't need Blueprint timers or hand-authored delays.
Create a MetaSound Source in the Content Browser, choose a mono output layout and open it. Import three short Wave Assets if you don't already have them.
Search AP: Sequence Wave Player in the add-node menu. This is in AudioPhysx → Playback.
Expand Sequence Waves to three inputs. Assign the click, movement and clunk in that order. These are individual Wave Assets, not arrays.
Connect the Source's On Play to the node's Play, and connect Out Mono to the Source's mono audio output.

If you want the Source to finish when the last recording ends, connect the player's On Finished to the Source's completion input. If you later add a tail-generating effect, move completion handling to the last effect.

A single Play creates three sounds in order. If you lengthen the middle recording, the final clunk should occur later automatically. If you turn on Loop Sequence, the whole pattern starts again; without looping, the player finishes after the final valid slot.
Replace the final clunk with a different-length recording and audition again. You'll immediately see why this approach is easier than maintaining hand-calculated trigger delays.

l: When this is the wrong node
p: If each stage needs to select a different random take, use Random Sequence Wave Player. If you need shots at fixed RPM while the trigger is held, use Start Loop End Player.

l: Signals, events and the end of a sound
p: Many AudioPhysx graph problems aren't about decoding audio; they're about confusing an event, an audio stream, and a lifecycle signal. Understanding these three concepts will make every node easier to use.

Play means start now. Stop generally cancels playback. Stop Firing means the held action has ended—play the release phase. These commands are intentionally different. For example, the Start Loop End Player should normally receive a Stop Firing event so it can play the outro.

Once a recording is started, the MetaSound audio output carries samples every audio-processing block. A trigger pin is not a wire containing the sound. A separate Out Mono or Audio pin carries that sample stream.

l: Completion belongs to the last audible stage
p: Consider this chain:

The original Wave Player can finish before the reflection taps have died away. If its On Finished directly ends the MetaSound Source, the reflection tail may be cut short. Route completion through the processor responsible for the last audible tail when it provides completion signals.
Similarly, stopping intentionally is not necessarily the same as finishing naturally. Don't assume every Stop will emit On Finished; check the particular player's documentation.

Some AudioPhysx nodes let you add more Wave slots, step arrays or distance ranges. The graph's pin layout is therefore part of the authored asset. Changing global Surface Audio routes can also change generated pins for Surface Wave Player. Back up and inspect affected graphs after those settings change.

A Source that loops forever should not be wired as though it has a natural ending after one recording. For held interactions, decide separately which event begins the sound, which event releases it, and what really marks the end of the audible result.

AudioPhysx extends MetaSounds with native C++ nodes for playing, processing and controlling sound. Choosing the right category is easier when you begin with the question you want your audio to answer.

l: I want to play recordings more intelligently
p: Do you need a random variation? A guaranteed order? Multiple simultaneous layers? A start/hold/end action? Explore Playback, which contains the integrated Wave Players.

l: I want the room or material to change the sound
p: You may need a filter, transmission model, directivity effect or reflection taps rather than another recording. Those tools are under Acoustics.

l: I want motion and travel time to matter
p: When a source moves or becomes more distant, sound arrival and spectral balance can change. Propagation contains distance delay, Doppler-style control and atmospheric absorption.

l: I want simpler trigger and control logic
p: Use QoL for routing triggers, smoothing values and managing trigger repetition. These nodes generally do not decode Wave Assets.

Every reference starts with what happens, then shows a game-audio use case and wiring steps. The exact pin list is folded away under Full input reference / Full output reference so you can still look up types without interrupting the explanation.
Understanding completion · Blueprint integration
Playback nodes select, schedule and combine recordings. Use them when a sound needs a behaviour more involved than simply playing one Wave Asset when it receives a trigger.

Random Wave Player chooses a recording when an event occurs, with optional no-immediate-repeat and overlap settings. Shuffle-Bag Wave Player is preferable when repeated events should gradually cover the available takes rather than picking freely every time.
A footstep or repeated impact often starts here.
Sequence Wave Player plays fixed recordings consecutively. Random Sequence Wave Player does the same but chooses a variation from an array at each step.
Layered Wave Player is different: it combines several layers within one event, optionally with small offsets. Choose sequence for one after another and layers for sounds together.

Start Loop End Player handles attack, held middle and release. At RPM = 0, middle recordings follow one another; with a positive RPM, overlapping shots start at a designed rate. See the automatic weapon walkthrough.

Use Distance Wave Player when near and far recordings differ, Surface Wave Player when Unreal surface types determine the material sound, and PhysMat Wave Player when exact Physical Material paths matter.
For near-miss projectiles, Flyby Wave Player is driven by a separate game-side calculation; it is not a generic Wave Player for every distant shot.

If the sound needs to be selected, choose a variation player. If it needs to happen in stages, choose a sequence. If it needs to continue while held, choose Start Loop End. If it needs to change with the game world, choose a distance or material-aware player.

l: Acoustics — change the character of sound
p: These nodes are for effects that can make the same recording behave differently in different spaces, behind different materials or at different listener positions. They are useful where another random recording is not enough.

Material Transmission uses an obstruction state and frequency-dependent losses to produce a muffled, transmitted sound. Use it for a simple, authored blocked/unblocked effect. Acoustic Paths instead consumes the selected route from the world solver, including route delay and three-band loss.
Early Reflections suggests the first short echoes from nearby surfaces. It uses a lightweight model controlled by room size and damping, not real-time geometric reconstruction.
Source Directivity shapes loudness and brightness as the listener moves from a source's front to its rear. It needs source-listener orientation information from the game.
Impact Dynamics turns an impact event plus a strength value into filtered and transient-shaped playback. It is an audio processor, not an impact detector.
Unreal attenuation and other environmental effects can also apply occlusion, air absorption and directivity. Compare the complete signal path before stacking several strong filters.
Browse the Acoustics reference · Try the obstruction recipe

When we see an explosion far away, the light arrives almost immediately while the sound takes time. A moving vehicle can change the apparent pitch and travel time of its sound. These nodes provide controllable approximations of those behaviours.

Distance Delay is suited to events where a chosen distance can be latched into a travel-time delay. Dynamic Propagation is designed for continuously updated distance and includes smoothing and jump handling.
Doppler Ratio outputs a control value based on radial motion; it does not render audio by itself. Atmosphere Absorption adjusts how frequencies are lost with travel through air.

A radial velocity is movement toward or away from the listener; total movement speed is not sufficient on its own. A distance supplied in centimetres must be converted to metres where a model explicitly expects metres. A sound travelling through air cannot meaningfully exceed the delay buffer that its node allocated.
Use a clean, short impact and an explicit Distance (cm) input with Distance Delay. Once that sounds correct, move to Dynamic Propagation and a moving-source recording.

l: QoL — small controls that clean up large graphs
p: These nodes deal mainly with events and numbers, not audio samples. Their purpose is to replace common branches, random checks and smoothing networks that would otherwise appear in every MetaSound.

Trigger Cooldown prevents rapid bursts from turning into dozens of audible events. Trigger Probability lets an event through at a configurable chance. Use them on optional rattles, contact ticks and other sounds that should not happen every time.
Float Smoother prevents block-rate control values from stepping abruptly. This is useful for engine load, filtering and environmental controls.
Distance Switch (Dynamic) routes a trigger to one distance band. It is a branching tool, whereas Distance Wave Player actually decodes recordings selected by distance.
The cooldown controls frequency, the probability controls whether the optional detail happens, and the player handles the recording. You can remove either control if it adds no value to the result.

A Wave Player can play a recording with only a trigger, but an acoustic processor needs to know something about the world: distance, material, obstruction, source direction or environment. AudioPhysx has interfaces and parameter names that link those game-side calculations to a MetaSound graph.
The current source uses one compact Float Array named AP.AcousticRoute.Selected. Its four values are ordered as follows:

The game-world solver decides which route to use. AP: Acoustic Paths reads that selected route and renders the corresponding delayed and filtered mono audio. This avoids connecting several unrelated route controls and accidentally using values from different world updates.

c: [delay in ms, low-band loss in dB, mid-band loss in dB, high-band loss in dB]

p: If you swap the low- and high-loss values, the filter could make the source sound brighter when the material should muffle it. If you pass seconds as milliseconds, a travel delay can be wrong by a factor of a thousand. Treat the array as a data contract, not a bag of arbitrary floats.

The source also contains propagation, atmosphere, transmission and impact parameters. These are registered by AudioPhysx's native interfaces and world/Blueprint helpers. Prefer the exact pins and interface versions supplied by the installed plugin over manually recreating near-identical parameters with different names.

The standalone flyby subsystem supplies five named Float parameters, listed on the Flyby Blueprint guide. Those must be exposed with matching names so the world helper can populate them before playback.

When changing engine or plugin versions, inspect a saved graph's generated MetaSound inputs before resaving it, especially if interface versions or surface-route settings changed. A graph can compile but listen to the wrong input if names or types no longer match.

The gameplay solver estimates a selected acoustic route between source and listener. The result is packed into four floating-point values: delay milliseconds, low-band loss dB, mid-band loss dB, and high-band loss dB. This node consumes that array and applies an audible delay and frequency-dependent reduction to the mono input.

The key design choice is that it renders one chosen route. It does not create two independent copies for direct and around-corner sound, which helps prevent phasey doubling and uncontrolled extra voices.

Place a sound on the other side of a wall with a doorway nearby. Compare a clear direct path with an obstructed one and an available around-door route. Observe how the delay and band losses change in the route data, then listen for the difference.
Feed your existing mono playback into Audio In.
Provide the four-value Selected Route array, preferably from the Acoustic Path Blueprint/world subsystem integration.

Early reflections are the first distinct sound returns from nearby surfaces: what you hear just after a clap in a small room. This node creates an approximate reflection pattern from a room-size control and the speed of sound, mixing it with the direct input.
It is a deliberate lightweight acoustic model. It helps make a dry recording feel placed in a space, but it does not trace walls or replace a full reverb for long late tails.

An impact is more than a volume change. Soft contacts tend to have gentler transients, while harder contacts can sound brighter and more aggressive. This node uses an Impact trigger and a normalized strength value to drive impact-time gain, filtering and transient emphasis around the input recording.
It is a sound-shaping node, not a collision detector. Supply the actual impact event and, if desired, calculate its strength through an existing AudioPhysx Blueprint helper.

Use one moderately strong metal knock recording. Audition it with an impact strength near the soft end and then near the hard end. Adjust the soft/hard gain and cutoff controls until one source asset provides useful expressive variation.

An obstructing material often reduces high frequencies more than lows. Rather than muting a source, this node uses authored low-band and high-band attenuation, a crossover and thickness-related controls to shape the sound that passes through a barrier.
The node needs an external Obstructed state and material information. It does not perform collision traces itself; it makes a mono signal respond to data supplied by your game.

A speaker, exhaust or human voice does not radiate identically in every direction. The node receives an angle between source orientation and the listener and uses it to shape both loudness and spectral content.

It separates broad rear attenuation from lower-frequency directivity. That matters because bass energy tends to remain more omnidirectional than high-frequency detail in many real sources; the node gives you an accessible way to suggest that effect.

Put a radio or machine in a test level and walk around it. Feed the changing listener-relative angle into the MetaSound. Listen for the brightness and loudness changing between the front and the back without a sudden on/off switch.

The node groups recordings into distance ranges. At playback time, it checks Distance (cm) and selects the matching range, then chooses a suitable recording from that range. This is about selecting a different recording, not merely making the same file quieter.

Close recordings may contain strong mechanical detail; far recordings can instead emphasize the report and environment. The dynamic range entries let a designer author those perspectives without building a large branching graph.

Prepare a close gunshot, a medium-distance gunshot and a distant report. Put the files into suitable bands; then change Distance (cm) before Play. Confirm the selected recording changes when the listener crosses each authored threshold.
Expand and configure your distance ranges in ascending order of Start Distance (cm).
Put a Waves array in each band and supply Distance (cm) from your existing distance system.
Use Play to request a sound. Set Max Distance (cm) and range Volume as needed, then audition the band transitions.

Play an opening sound, sustain a repeatable middle section, and finish with a proper release when the action ends.

This node follows three phases: Start, Middle, and End. Each phase chooses a recording from its respective Wave Asset Array. It works for automatic weapons, powered tools, long energy effects, and other actions that start, continue, then stop.

The important distinction is RPM. At RPM = 0, middle recordings play consecutively when each recording finishes. At a positive RPM, the node schedules fresh middle recordings at a fixed number of starts per minute, so the recordings can overlap. The implementation maintains a bounded pool of twelve middle voices instead of dynamically creating a new audio player for every shot.

For a rifle, put an initial bolt/attack in Start Waves, several shot bodies in Loop Waves, and mechanical release recordings in End Waves. Set RPM to 600: a new middle shot is scheduled approximately every 100 milliseconds once the intro finishes. Then send Stop Firing and listen to the ending.

A MetaSound Float input may change in discrete blocks even when the game value is continuous. Feeding those updates directly into a filter or mix control can create stepping. Float Smoother gradually approaches a target using separate rise and fall responses.
It operates at control/block rate, so think of it as a parameter-conditioning tool, not an audio-waveform filter.
Connect a changing engine-load value to Target. Give increasing values a short Rise (ms) and decreasing values a longer Fall (ms) so the motor reacts quickly to throttle but relaxes more slowly.
Connect the changing Float to Target.
Set independent Rise (ms) and Fall (ms) values. Start with modest values and judge them by ear.
Use Smoothed wherever a downstream node expects the stabilized control. Use Snap when a level or state change should happen immediately.
Rise (ms) and Fall (ms) are smoothing time constants rather than fixed delays. Zero snaps immediately in the corresponding direction. Snap overrides the gradual transition for the current target.

Because the output is block-rate, it should not be mistaken for sample-by-sample modulation of an audio buffer.

Collision, interaction and animation systems often produce more triggers than a sound designer wants to hear. This node lets an input trigger through, then holds off additional events for a configurable period.
The purpose is practical: avoid six identical scrape clicks caused by one contact, or a machine noise retriggering faster than it can be perceived.
Send repeated footstep events to In with a modest Cooldown (ms). Observe which events reach On Passed and which are rejected. Then set Cooldown (ms) to zero to compare unrestricted behaviour.
Connect a source trigger to In.
Choose Cooldown (ms) for the event you want to limit.
Use On Passed to start playback; optionally inspect rejected events when debugging. Reset clears the cooldown state.

Not every event needs an audible consequence. A subtle rattle might happen on some movements, a cloth rustle on occasional animation cycles, or a debris tick on only a fraction of impacts.

Add a faint gear-rattle layer to a running machine, but send its trigger through this node first. A probability of 0 should never pass; 1 should always pass; values between those extremes should create occasional events.
Send an event trigger to In.

MetaSound processes audio, but it does not automatically know where the player is standing, what material a bullet passed, or whether a source is behind a wall. AudioPhysx provides Blueprint-facing functions and components so you can feed that information into the sound graph.

The division is intentional: world queries and gameplay events run outside the audio rendering loop, while the MetaSound node uses the resulting values to select or process a sound. You don't need to use every integration feature to benefit from the Playback nodes.

Start by printing the Blueprint's distance, material or route result. Confirm it changes as expected in your level before spending time debugging the MetaSound. This keeps gameplay-data problems separate from audio-rendering problems.

A good near-miss sound is about where the projectile passed and when the listener would hear it, not simply whether the weapon fired. AudioPhysx lets you submit a straight path segment and evaluate the closest approach without setting up Chaos physics or spawning special audio-specific bullet Actors.
The integration has two parts: a game-side helper decides whether and when a close pass is audible; AP: Flyby Wave Player renders the whizz and optional crack from your supplied recordings.

Imagine a bullet travelling along a line that passes beside the listener. The nearest point on that line is its closest approach. If that point is inside the configured audible radius, the event may qualify as a flyby. The helper also estimates arrival time and whether the configured speed and geometry permit a shock-wave effect.

AP: Calculate Flyby returns an FAPFlybyResult containing bAudible, bShockWave, ClosestPoint, DistanceMeters, SpeedMetersPerSecond, Intensity and ArrivalSeconds. This function is useful for debugging the geometry before requesting playback.
AP: Play Projectile Flyby performs the test and submits an accepted sound for scheduling. Its Boolean return means accepted for scheduling, not that the player has already heard the clip.
Make a MetaSound Source that will be used only for flyby playback. Add AP: Flyby Wave Player from the Playback category.
Fill Whizz Waves with your licensed near-miss variations. Fill Crack Waves if you want a separate supersonic shock layer. Short, clearly edited samples make debugging easier.
Connect the Source's On Play to the Flyby player's Play, its Out Mono to the Source output, and route completion appropriately.
Use the exact names below. Connect them to the corresponding Flyby Wave Player controls; they are set by the world subsystem before the sound starts.
Test the MetaSound manually with reasonable values first. Then use it as the asset supplied to the Blueprint helper.
AP.Flyby.DistanceM → Distance (m). Closest distance from the projectile path to the listener, in metres.
AP.Flyby.SpeedMps → Speed (m/s). Projectile speed, in metres per second.
AP.Flyby.Intensity → Intensity. The computed strength control.
AP.Flyby.SpeedOfSoundMps → Speed of Sound (m/s). Acoustic model speed in metres per second.
AP.Flyby.Shock → Shock. A Float gate, typically 1 for requested crack and 0 otherwise.
The parameter names above come from the reviewed APFlybyWorldSubsystem.cpp development source. Keep them identical in the MetaSound graph.
Use the weapon muzzle world location for PathStart and the trace hit point (or maximum trace end) for PathEnd.
Provide ProjectileSpeedMps in metres per second, even though Unreal's path vectors are world units in centimetres.
Pass your flyby MetaSound Source as FlybyMetaSound and choose an AudibleRadiusM appropriate to your test.
Call AP: Play Projectile Flyby once per hitscan shot. PathAgeSeconds is zero for a fresh, instantaneous hitscan query.
Shoot beside the listener, then farther away than the radius. Watch the Boolean acceptance result and listen for the corresponding audio behaviour.

For a projectile that has already moved, send consecutive start/end positions rather than predicting its whole future path. The optional ProjectileInstance should uniquely identify that specific projectile so the system can suppress duplicate near-miss events. A shared weapon object is not a suitable substitute when it fires multiple independent bullets.

PathAgeSeconds describes how old the reported movement segment is. The source comments recommend using segment length divided by projectile speed for a segment submitted after motion, so that scheduling can account for already elapsed travel time.

This first version assumes a simplified constant-speed path and approximate acoustic arrival. It positions playback near the closest approach; it does not perform a continuous 3D flyby simulation or exact shock-front tracing. Test very close passes, fast shots and different listener positions in your game before treating timings as final.

You don't need a dedicated audio Actor to use every AudioPhysx feature. The public Blueprint library provides convenient entry points for sounds at world locations and for registering existing audio components with the plugin's managed update system.

l: Play a sound at a world position
p: AP: Play Physical Sound accepts a sound asset, world location and source rotation, with volume and optional acoustic/obstruction behaviour exposed by its Blueprint function. This is suitable when the game already knows where an event happened, such as a door slam or explosion.
AP: Play Physical Impact is the related convenience operation when you already have an FHitResult. It can use hit-location information rather than requiring you to reconstruct the position by hand.
Neither operation creates a sound recording. You still supply a USoundBase, usually a prepared MetaSound Source or other Unreal sound asset.

l: Keep an existing Audio Component updated
p: AP: Register Audio Component associates an existing UAudioComponent with managed AudioPhysx parameter updates. The registration call allows obstruction tracing to be enabled or disabled. AP: Unregister Audio Component removes it from that management when it is no longer required.

This is useful for persistent emitters, where creating a new sound for every update would be inappropriate. Registration should follow the component's lifetime so the world subsystem does not keep attempting work on an irrelevant emitter.

AP: Set World Environment supplies temperature, humidity and pressure values for the AudioPhysx world context. These are used by relevant acoustic processing paths; they do not, on their own, change every sound in the game.

Create a mono MetaSound Source with a simple Wave Player, call AP: Play Physical Sound at a known location, and verify that it is audible with expected spatialization. Once basic playback works, enable acoustic processing and compare with an unobstructed control sound.

The helper requires a valid world/audio environment and a supported sound asset. If you're debugging a silent sound, test the MetaSound directly before assuming the Blueprint's acoustic query is at fault.

A direct ray between a speaker and listener may cross a barrier. In some scenes, sound could instead travel through an opening or around an obstacle. AudioPhysx's path solver provides a game-thread approximation of that situation, producing an acoustic route that the MetaSound can render.

AP: Query Acoustic Path is exposed through UAPAcousticPathLibrary. Give it a world context, source position, listener position and optionally a source actor. The returned FAPAcousticPathResult describes direct-path obstruction, delay and low/mid/high frequency losses. It can also describe an alternative route, including its proposed emitter location and losses, when one is valid.
The flags are important:
bAroundPathValid means the solver found a usable alternate candidate.
bAroundPathSelected means the system considers that alternate preferable to the direct path.
A valid path is not automatically the path selected for playback. This distinction helps prevent two sound copies playing at once merely because a doorway route exists.
Use a source on one side of a simple wall and a listener on the other. Leave a doorway or other controllable opening so there is a meaningful alternate route to compare.
Call AP: Query Acoustic Path and print direct obstruction, selected-route state, delays and the loss values.
Move the listener to a clear line of sight, then behind the wall, then near the doorway. Confirm the results change in a way that matches the geometry.
Use the compact selected-route Float Array with AP: Acoustic Paths. Listen to the difference only after the geometric result makes sense.

World traces require access to scene geometry. They belong on the game thread, not inside a DSP function rendering thousands of audio samples. The managed AudioPhysx world subsystem provides limits and scheduling controls so a large level does not perform unconstrained acoustic queries for every source at every moment.
When a sound seems too muffled, print the selected route first. If the wrong barrier is being found, changing the MetaSound filter will only hide the real problem.

AudioPhysx has components that connect real game objects to the acoustic model. You don't need all of them for ordinary playback. They're most useful when you want source-to-listener obstruction or around-opening behaviour to react to the level.

l: The emitter: where the sound begins
p: UAPSpatialAudioEmitterComponent represents a managed sound source with its audio and optional attenuation behaviour. It can participate in obstruction updates, allowing the sound to react as the listener and environment change.

l: The barrier: what blocks the sound
p: UAPAcousticBarrierComponent associates thickness and acoustic material information with a primitive. Its model is more descriptive than treating a wall as simply “blocked or clear.” The associated geometry and collision still have to be set up correctly in the map.

l: The portal: where an alternate path may exist
p: UAPAcousticPortalComponent represents an opening or passage with extra frequency-band loss. An around-path candidate can use it when the world path solver supports that route. This is not a full room impulse-response or reverberation bake.

UAPPhysicsBridgeComponent connects movement, transmission and environment-related information to audio. The exact configuration depends on the emitter and game system; this is not a requirement for simple Wave Player nodes.

Build two simple rooms, a doorway and one looping source. Add an acoustic barrier to a relevant primitive and a portal near the opening. Move the listener between clear line of sight, obstructed position and doorway. Inspect the path query result before adjusting how the MetaSound renders it.

Acoustic tracing is scheduled and budgeted. Begin with just one emitter, then profile how the subsystem scales with your expected number of active sources rather than enabling high-frequency traces on everything.

An acoustic material describes how an authored surface should affect sound. It is not a recording and is not automatically measured from your level geometry. The values express a model that AudioPhysx can use when estimating transmission and other acoustic behaviour.

UAPAcousticPhysicalMaterial extends Unreal's Physical Material with acoustic properties. It can include material density and longitudinal sound speed, damping, a thickness context and low/mid/high authored transmission losses. There are also absorption and scattering controls for acoustic models that use them.

l: Think in terms of listening results
p: A heavy, sealed barrier may need much larger transmission loss than a thin partition. That loss can differ across frequency bands; the goal is to make obstructed audio believable, not to pretend every wall is accurately described by one physical constant.

You can use an authored three-band loss curve or the available approximate mass-law model. Authored values are useful when you want repeatable, designer-controlled outcomes. The mass-law option is a simplified estimate, not a measurement of a specific finished structure.

UAPAudioSettings contains environment and workload controls, including world update scheduling, obstruction-ray limits, maximum path detail and optional alternate-route processing. These matter when the scene contains many emitters: a convincing effect that performs poorly with twenty active sources is not ready for shipping.

AP: Surface Wave Player can generate pins based on enabled surface routes in AudioPhysx settings. If you change that list, restart the editor and review existing MetaSound graphs. Unlike a runtime float value, a changed pin layout can affect authored graph connections.

Every recipe here starts with a sound-design goal, not a list of API calls. You can follow a short graph, listen for a specific result, and then explore the deeper node reference when you want more control.

These examples describe how to wire and test AudioPhysx. They do not include or grant rights to sound recordings. Use licensed or original Wave Assets and check their loudness and edit points before judging the node's result.

l: A one-shot that doesn't sound identical every time
p: Goal: Make footsteps, impacts or small interactions feel less repetitive by varying the recording instead of triggering one identical file on every event.

Import four or five takes of the same type of event. For example, several small metal knocks. Trim obvious leading silence, match the perceived loudness where practical and keep them in a single Wave Asset Array.
Create a mono MetaSound Source and add AP: Random Wave Player.
Connect your Wave Asset Array to Waves, then connect Play from the desired trigger event.
Connect Out Mono to the Source output, enable No Immediate Repeat if desired and audition repeated starts.
Trigger faster than one recording can finish. Check Max Voices and decide how much overlapping sound the game needs.

A convincing variation player should sound natural, not simply more random. If one take is much louder than the others, listeners may notice the level jump more than they appreciate the variety. If you need each variation to be heard within a cycle, try the Shuffle-Bag Wave Player.
Goal: Start a weapon with an attack recording, repeat variable shot bodies at an actual firing rate, and play a proper release tail when the player lets go of the trigger.

The important improvement over a simple sequential player is that a shot recording might last longer than the interval between rounds. RPM controls when the next shot begins, not how quickly the current recording must finish.

Start Waves should contain the distinctive attack or mechanism sound when the weapon first fires. Loop Waves holds your repeatable middle gunshot variations. End Waves contains the release, stopping mechanism or tail used after firing stops.
Create a mono MetaSound Source and add AP: Start Loop End Player.
Fill Start Waves, Loop Waves and End Waves. Use multiple middle takes to prevent the same shot being selected endlessly.
Set RPM to 600 for a nominal 100 ms interval between middle-shot starts. Positive RPM values are distinct from the RPM = 0 completion-driven mode.
Send the weapon pressed event to Start Firing and the released event to Stop Firing. Connect Out Mono to the graph output and completion as appropriate.
With Immediate Release enabled, active shots fade and the end begins promptly. With it disabled, active audio gets time to complete first.

At 600 RPM, a new middle recording should start approximately every tenth of a second once the intro has finished, even when an individual recording is longer. Releasing the weapon should prevent new middle shots and lead into an ending. Because the node has a twelve-voice middle pool, very long samples at high RPM can exhaust the available voices; new shot starts may then be skipped rather than cutting earlier recordings off.
If your gameplay only sends Start Firing and never sends Stop Firing, the source may remain in the active middle state. This is a gameplay trigger contract, not a playback bug.
Detailed player reference
Goal: Keep the order of a sound effect recognizable while allowing its individual details to change.

Imagine a mechanical device that opens, performs an action, then closes. A random single-sound player cannot enforce that three-stage structure; a fixed sequence can, but it sounds the same every time. AP: Random Sequence Wave Player combines both ideas.
Create one array of opening clicks, one of mechanical middle actions and one of ending clunks. Each array can contain multiple takes, but keep each array specific to its stage.
Create a mono Source, add AP: Random Sequence Wave Player and expand the Sequence Steps group to three stages.
Connect the opening array to stage one, mechanism array to stage two, and ending array to stage three.
Connect Play and Out Mono. Use On Finished if this effect should end the Source when the third recording finishes.
The recordings within each stage should vary, but the opening, middle and ending should always follow one another in that order.

l: Why there are no delay pins
p: This is a completion-driven sequencer. The next stage starts when the current recording ends. If you make the middle clip longer, the final stage happens later automatically. For simultaneous layers, choose a Layered Wave Player instead.
Goal: Make a footstep choose the correct texture—stone, grass, metal or another material—based on what the player actually stepped on.

AudioPhysx does not automatically perform the footstep trace inside the Wave Player. Your character, animation system or Blueprint sends the surface identifier. The player then selects a recording pool for that surface.

l: Choose how to identify a material
p: Use AP: Surface Wave Player when Unreal's physical-surface type is enough. It is useful for broadly defined categories such as grass, gravel or metal.
The node's dynamic surface routes may depend on AudioPhysx project settings. Configure those before authoring a large number of graphs.
Use AP: PhysMat Wave Player when multiple surfaces share a type but still need distinct sound choices. It compares the full Physical Material asset path rather than just a category number.
At the foot contact moment, trace or otherwise identify the Physical Material of the ground. Confirm the gameplay query returns material information as intended.
Use the surface type for Surface Wave Player, or the exact material asset path for PhysMat Wave Player. Supply it before firing Play.
Assign multiple Wave Assets for each surface and fill default recordings for unknown or unmapped surfaces.
Walk across the boundary while watching the returned material data. Confirm the recordings follow the ground and that unmatched materials fall back sensibly.

A good footstep system also depends on which recording is chosen and when. Keep variation within a surface coherent, align transients so feet land on time, and avoid overloading the node with sounds for every gameplay state. Movement speed and footwear can be handled by additional routing if needed.

l: A projectile passing close to the listener
p: Goal: Hear an appropriate flyby when a projectile passes nearby, without playing a near-miss sound for every shot in the level.

The trick is to test the projectile's path, not merely its firing event. AudioPhysx can estimate closest approach from a submitted segment and, for accepted near misses, schedule playback near that point.
A mono MetaSound Source containing AP: Flyby Wave Player, whizz and optional crack Wave Asset Arrays, and a Blueprint that knows the projectile's path start, path end and nominal speed.
Wire the five runtime Float parameters described in the flyby Blueprint guide. Confirm the player auditions with manual values first.
Call AP: Play Projectile Flyby with a path that passes near the listener, within AudibleRadiusM.
Keep the speed and recording the same, but move the path outside the audible radius. This should not be accepted as a near miss.
Change the supplied speed while keeping the geometry comparable. The crack layer depends on the calculated shock condition, not simply the presence of a bullet recording.

Positions are in Unreal world units (normally centimetres), but ProjectileSpeedMps and AudibleRadiusM are in metres per second and metres. Mixing units can make a believable path look thousands of times too far away or too fast.
This is a useful game-audio approximation, not a complete aerodynamic shock-wave simulation. Test timing and source placement in your actual gameplay level.

l: Make a sound believable behind a wall
p: Goal: Have a mono sound change its tone and apparent arrival when the path between source and listener becomes obstructed.

A hard on/off mute is rarely convincing. Even when an object blocks line of sight, some sound can transmit through the barrier or reach the listener by another route. AudioPhysx gives you two levels of control depending on whether the game already has acoustic path data.
Use AP: Material Transmission when you can provide an Obstructed Boolean plus designer-authored frequency losses. This is the easiest demonstration: toggle one state and hear a darker, quieter sound.
Use AP: Acoustic Paths when the Blueprint/world solver supplies a four-value selected-route array. It can represent delay and three-band loss for the preferred direct or around-obstacle route.
A spoken phrase or a short repeated impact with some high-frequency content makes obstruction changes easy to hear.
Play it in an open path with no extra obstruction treatment. Adjust your game attenuation separately if necessary.
Wire the appropriate node and its controls. Compare clear and blocked values, keeping the recording itself unchanged.
If the selected processor can delay the audio, use its completion output so the tail isn't cut off when the original Wave Player finishes.

If the obstructed version sounds like someone turned the volume down but left all the sharp high frequencies untouched, it probably needs more spectral coloration. If it becomes completely dull, examine whether you're applying both Unreal occlusion and full-strength AudioPhysx transmission loss.

Most AudioPhysx issues fall into three groups: a node was not installed or registered correctly; a playback graph has missing triggers or Wave Assets; or a world-driven node receives data in the wrong units or order.
Start with the Troubleshooting guide. It separates basic audio problems from build and packaged-game issues, so you can diagnose the smallest possible part of the system.

A useful report says what Unreal Engine and plugin version you're using, how to reproduce the sound or compile issue, and what you expected to happen. Include the first meaningful compiler error or a small screenshot of the relevant MetaSound connections rather than only the final error message.

When something goes wrong, isolate the system in this order: can Unreal play the asset? → does the MetaSound receive a trigger? → does the node output audio? → are world parameters correct? Debugging each layer separately is usually faster than changing every setting at once.

l: I can't find any AudioPhysx nodes
p: Open Edit → Plugins and verify AudioPhysx is enabled. Restart the Editor after plugin activation or a native rebuild. In a MetaSound Source, search AP: and inspect the AudioPhysx categories.

For source builds, confirm the full plugin directory includes the .uplugin descriptor and that its C++ module actually compiled for your installed engine version. Copying a standalone Source folder is not equivalent to installing a complete code plugin.

Start with a simple mono MetaSound Source and one known-good Wave Asset. Connect Play and Out Mono before adding other processing. Check that the array is not empty and that the recording imports and auditions normally in Unreal.

If the sound plays in a simple Source but disappears in your game, examine attenuation, concurrency and world-space source position. If it stops when you add an acoustic effect, inspect that effect's input values and the completion routing.

l: The sequence plays only the first recording
p: For a fixed or random sequence, make sure later slots contain playable Wave Assets and are genuinely part of the expandable group. The next sound should follow playback completion, not a manually connected delay. Check whether an early Source-level On Finished is terminating the graph.

A held sequence is expected to keep its middle phase active while firing. Stop Firing is required to request the end phase. Immediate Release controls whether active recordings fade promptly or finish first. At positive RPM values, overlapping middle voices can remain audible after the release request when immediate release is disabled.

Print the result from AP: Calculate Flyby before requesting playback. Check that the shot path passes within AudibleRadiusM, that path positions are in Unreal world units, and that speed is supplied in metres per second.
If geometry is accepted but audio remains silent, verify the five named external Float inputs in the flyby MetaSound and whether its On Play reaches the Wave Player.

l: The acoustic path sounds too dark or delayed
p: Inspect the four selected-route values: delay ms, low loss dB, mid loss dB, high loss dB. Check that Unreal occlusion or air absorption is not doubling the effect, and confirm the requested delay is within the node's allocated capacity.

When you edit the enabled surface-route list, AP: Surface Wave Player may expose a different pin layout. Back up the affected MetaSounds, restart after changing settings, and inspect connections before resaving. For an ordinary expandable group, verify the authored group instance count remains correct.

l: C++ errors after a source update
p: Read the first compiler error, not only the final build summary. Close the Editor, disable Live Coding and make sure you have not kept two versions of the same node .cpp under different names. If generated reflection files are stale, remove the plugin's Binaries and Intermediate directories before regenerating/rebuilding.

l: The Editor works but a packaged game doesn't
p: A clean Editor build is not proof of a working Shipping build. Check that assets were cooked, the runtime module loads, all references are included, and any optional audio system or config used by the graph is available at runtime. Begin with a packaged Development build for useful logging, then verify the same behaviour in Shipping.

l: What to include in a useful bug report
p: Exact Unreal Engine version, plugin version, operating system and build configuration.
Which MetaSound node or Blueprint helper failed.
A minimal graph or path setup with reproducible inputs.
Expected result, actual result and first relevant log message.

l: Is AudioPhysx a replacement for MetaSounds or Unreal Audio?
p: No. It provides additional C++ nodes and Blueprint integration for the existing Unreal audio pipeline. You still use MetaSound Sources, the mixer, spatialization, Sound Attenuation and concurrency features as appropriate for your game.

l: Why are so many outputs mono?
p: Mono is a practical source format for many spatial game sounds. It lets Unreal handle the source's 3D positioning and means an acoustic processor can work on one clearly defined signal. It does not mean every sound in your game must be mono.

l: Does it generate all realistic audio procedurally?
p: No. Many nodes play or transform your own recordings. The physically inspired processors model particular behaviours such as attenuation, delay, directionality or early reflections; they are not a complete acoustic simulation of the game world.

l: What's the difference between Surface and PhysMat playback?
p: Surface Wave Player chooses from a category such as a physical-surface type. PhysMat Wave Player can distinguish specific Physical Material asset paths. Use the broader category when the sound should be shared across several surfaces, and the exact path when you need a more detailed selection.

l: Why doesn't Stop always fire On Finished?
p: Stop can mean an explicit cancellation. Natural completion means the recording has actually ended. Some nodes distinguish those two behaviours so gameplay can tell the difference. Read the particular player's reference before wiring Source completion.

l: Can I use a Sound Cue instead of MetaSound?
p: Unreal's native Sound Cues can still be used wherever your workflow calls for them. AudioPhysx's custom Sound Cue QoL nodes are planned, not included in the reviewed development source. Current native node references are MetaSound-focused.

l: Will the plugin work in UE6 without updates?
p: No UE6 compatibility has been verified or promised. Native code plugins depend on engine APIs, and some current AudioPhysx player and dynamic-interface implementations use APIs with compatibility risks. Follow the published support matrix for the specific product version you intend to use.

l: Are acoustic material numbers scientifically measured?
p: Not by default. AudioPhysx offers authored and simplified modelling choices. Material values must be selected meaningfully for the game, and a convincing result is not the same thing as a validated laboratory measurement.
